samples.text: And I believe there can be only one response, to say, "Hands off the ICC and all those other institutions that protect the international legal order." Because the reality is that we still need to fight impunity. not least through the special tribunal for the crime of aggression against Ukraine, which the Netherlands has offered to host in The Hague. And let me be absolutely clear, we cannot accept impunity. In this fight, Ukraine has no choice but to defend itself. But Russia makes the choice every day to wage war. And Russia must be held to account for its flagrant violations of the UN Charter. for the immeasurable suffering inflicted on so many victims and families in this senseless war. And since the downing of flight MH17, the Netherlands has come to understand this only too well. And many others understand it too, with Russia threatening global food security and millions of people experiencing the consequences. And history teaches us that the only way to resolve conflict is through justice. That was the idea underpinning the establishment 80 years ago of the International Court of Justice, the principal judicial organ of the United Nations. And it's a conviction that is widely shared, as illustrated by the fact that more and more countries are finding their way to the ICJ. So let us all continue to stand up for what we have built and strengthen it further as we go forward. Ladies and gentlemen, cooperation is the cornerstone of our history, and cooperation is what the world expects of us, now and in the future. Take the question of how we handle AI. We face a choice. Do we let a small group of companies and countries take all the decisions while the rest of us simply look on? Or do we decide together, within the logical setting of the United Nations, what our future should look like? And it is also time for us to press forward together and tackle that other great challenge of our time, climate change.

Without the UN, which is often the only organization capable of supplying aid in the toughest places on the earth, millions of people will be deprived of food, clean water, and medical aid. Over the past 80 years, we've taken the UN's achievement for granted. We've neglected to look back on where we've come from and all the milestones we have achieved along the way. And although the situation right now might be especially difficult, I know this too, it has never been easy. Every achievement was preceded by the lengthy consultations. Countries were often at loggerheads, and sometimes we were attempting to throw in the towel, but that never happened. And the reason can only be that, despite our many differences, we all understand what's at stake. That's the context in which I feel the increasingly frank debate on the UN future. Yes, the world has changed. Yes, international relations have changed. And yes, the way we work together has changed. But I believe that this can lead us to only one conclusion. that we must change with times. And that's exactly what we're doing through initiatives like UN80, which aims to enhance the UN's impact on the ground, simplify structure, and forge stronger partnerships with other bodies, like international financial institutions, the private sector, and philanthropic organizations. Changing with the times also means making the most of today's opportunities. Early this week, I spoke with several UN youth representatives. They are growing up in a different time to you and me, with new concerns, but also new opportunities. We need their insights, not only because our decisions will affect their future, but above all, because they are the future. So if we are to move forward, we must work together by using AI and other technologies wherever possible. And the Kingdom of the Netherlands has already taken the lead on this by teaming up with donors and partners to explore new ways of boosting the efficiency and effectiveness of multilateral institutions. New ways, but not new principles.
